# Data Drives the Design {#sec-data}

The machinery is secondary. OO or functional, compiled or collected,
checked by `rustc` or by a constructor: those are how you pay for a
smaller set of demands.

**Names.** A curated vocabulary. Domain-driven design's ubiquitous
language, scaled to a package or to one developer's system, not reserved
for a program with the word "enterprise" in the brief. The names are the
model. If you cannot say the sentence without inventing a noun, the model
is missing a noun. If you have three nouns for one fact, the model is
avoiding a decision.

**Types.** A name admits only valid, structured values. The structure is
known. The meaning is the name, not the payload. An `integer64` that is
secretly a double is a tolerated lie at the physics layer; at the
vocabulary layer the name still has to mean a 64-bit integer, and the
verbs have to keep the lie from leaking. A `status` that is secretly any
string is a lie at the vocabulary layer, which is worse, because nothing
downstream can recover the five legal values by inspecting the SEXPTYPE.

**Views.** How a value appears is configurable in the best systems and
hand-written in R, and in both cases it is part of the contract. The view
is not the value. Format at the host.

**Verbs.** Functions do the work. Open dispatch attaches them to types
without trapping them inside types. A workflow is a composition of verbs
that values flow through. When a step needs identity --- a socket, a
token, a conversation --- the value flowing through is a handle, and the
handle is explicit.

**Data first.** The shapes in the domain drive the types. You do not
start from a class hierarchy you admired in another codebase and pour the
data in. You start from the record, the enum, the document, the event,
and you ask what must be true of each. The functions arrive when the
shapes can survive a round trip through a verb without losing a law.

```{mermaid}
flowchart TB
  subgraph domain [The domain]
    records[Records and documents]
    enums[Enumerations]
    events[Events and failures]
  end
  subgraph program [The program]
    parse[Parse at the boundary]
    values[Named values]
    verbs[Verbs]
    views[Views]
    handles[Handles]
  end
  records --> parse
  enums --> parse
  events --> parse
  parse --> values
  values --> verbs
  values --> views
  handles --> verbs
  verbs --> values
```

Everything earlier in the book is a detail under this picture.

The header, the three empties, cons against vectors, reference counts,
ALTREP, and promises explain why the values in the middle can be cheap
and still behave like values. The context chapter explains why a handle
is a different node, not a different mood. Signals explain how failures
and narration stay structured while the values move. The lineage explains
why the picture feels natural in R and slightly uphill to enforce. The
container rules are the picture applied to one API. The type chapter is
the picture applied to a language that will not write the boxes for you.
The appearance chapter is the view box, which people skip and users feel.

## What to stop arguing about

Whether a given package is "really OO" is not a useful argument. Whether
its names are curated, whether its constructors parse, whether its
printers tell the truth, and whether its verbs are open where a stranger
should be able to extend them: those are useful arguments. You can win
them in S3, in S7, in Rust, in PowerShell, in a disciplined corner of
Python. You can lose them in all five, loudly, with a lot of classes.

Composition over inheritance falls out of the same picture. Inheritance
bundles "what I am" with "what I can do" and with "how I am stored." The
picture wants those separable. A subtype is a real tool when the domain
has a real inclusion and the laws of the parent are laws of the child.
It is a bad tool when what you wanted was a new verb, or a new view, or
a nullable field. R's generic functions make the good case easy and the
bad case unnecessary. You can still build the bad case. The language is
not going to slap the metaphor out of your hand.

## The stance, small enough to reuse

Treat R as a Scheme-powered array language for having a conversation with
data. Let the conversation discover the nouns. Then make the nouns
boring: parsed, printable, and passed to verbs. Keep mutation in handles
at the edge. Keep foreign runtimes behind interfaces that exchange
objects and lifetimes, not surprise text. Pick one story for failure at
each boundary.

The value illusion is what makes the middle of that program pleasant. You
get to think in values while the runtime shares, delays, and sometimes
never allocates. The illusion is not permission to forget the edge. At
the edge, identity is real, the network is real, missingness is real, and
the user's eye is real. Name those too.

You were not messing around without a goal. You were checking, from the
node header upward, whether a taste you already had was compatible with
the machine you actually run. It is. The machine will not write the
program in that taste. It will only stop punishing you for it, provided
you stop asking a value to be a handle, a signal to be a string, and a
name to be a hope.
